morphology.shape: Amastigote (round/oval, intracellular) in humans; promastigote (elongated, flagellated) in the sandfly vector
morphology.size: Amastigotes ~2-5 µm; promastigotes ~15-30 µm including flagellum

protozoanDetails.lifeCycleForm: Amastigote (non-flagellated, intracellular within macrophages — the human/diagnostic tissue form) and promastigote (flagellated, extracellular — the sandfly-stage/culture form)

habitat.naturalHabitat: Reticuloendothelial system (spleen, liver, bone marrow) of the human/mammalian host; midgut of sandflies
habitat.hostAssociation: Zoonotic in some regions (dogs, rodents as reservoirs) and anthroponotic (human-to-sandfly-to-human) in others depending on the region
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Transmitted by female Phlebotomus (Old World) or Lutzomyia (New World) sandflies
habitat.reservoir: Infected humans and, in some regions, dogs and other mammals; sandfly vector

microscopy.stain: Giemsa stain of bone marrow, splenic, or lymph node aspirate
microscopy.appearance: Small, round-to-oval amastigotes with a nucleus and kinetoplast, seen within macrophages

culture.growthCharacteristics: Promastigote form grows in specialized media, used mainly in reference laboratories
culture.colonyMorphology: Not applicable — grows as motile promastigotes in liquid/biphasic medium

identificationClues: Amastigotes visualized within macrophages on Giemsa-stained bone marrow, spleen, or lymph node aspirate
Serology and PCR are increasingly used alongside or instead of invasive tissue sampling
Marked hepatosplenomegaly, fever, weight loss, and pancytopenia ("kala-azar," meaning "black fever") are classic clinical clues

diseases: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) — fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, wasting
Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (a later cutaneous complication in some patients)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Bite of an infected female sandfly (Phlebotomus species in the Old World)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Endemic to parts of the Indian subcontinent, East Africa, and Brazil; visceral leishmaniasis is fatal in the large majority of untreated cases
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Tissue aspirate microscopy (bone marrow being relatively safer than splenic aspirate) remains a key diagnostic method, though serology/PCR are increasingly favored where available

examFacts.importantTest: Giemsa-stained bone marrow/splenic aspirate showing amastigotes
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Causes systemic (visceral) disease with marked hepatosplenomegaly, unlike cutaneous Leishmania species
